claims.text: Catalytic activity in ethanol oxidation is governed by stabilization of adsorbed reaction intermediates through electronic interactions with the PGM surface.
Ethanol-oxidation selectivity is governed by stabilization of adsorbed reaction intermediates through electronic interactions with the PGM surface.
Catalyst durability is governed by stabilization of adsorbed reaction intermediates through electronic interactions with the PGM surface.
Adsorbed acetaldehyde and hydroxyl groups are particularly important intermediates governing ethanol-oxidation performance.
Alloying Pt or Pd nanoparticles with Ru or Ni can alter the d-band center of the PGM surface.
The PGM d-band center influences the adsorption strength and stability of ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
The PGM d-band center modulates the adsorption energies of acetaldehyde and hydroxyl species.
Moving the d-band center closer to the Fermi level strengthens intermediate binding.
Stronger intermediate binding produced by a d-band shift toward the Fermi level promotes catalytic activity.
Stronger intermediate binding produced by a d-band shift toward the Fermi level promotes selectivity.
Excessive stabilization of adsorbed intermediates can poison the catalyst and reduce durability.
Alloying that shifts the d-band center toward the Fermi level will improve ethanol-oxidation activity and selectivity up to an optimum.
Beyond the optimum d-band position, excessive intermediate stabilization will reduce durability through poisoning.
The relevant baseline is the unalloyed PGM catalyst tested under otherwise identical ethanol-oxidation conditions.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply in aqueous ethanol oxidation at moderate pH and ethanol concentration.
The proposed relationship may fail at extreme pH or in non-aqueous solvents because different reaction pathways can dominate.
X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy or density-functional-theory calculations can be used to determine or estimate the d-band-center position.
